title: Hongzhi, Part 2: Guidepost For The House Of Silent Illumination
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up Hongzhi's poems "Guidepost for the House of Silent Illumination" and "Guidepost for the Hall of Pure Bliss," reading them alongside Taigen's commentary. Starting from the question of what would actually help in a given situation, Eko turns to Hongzhi's image of the empty field, a rich field of non-separation that sesshin brings to life. Silence and illumination work together, and Vimalakirti's thunderous silence stays fully engaged in the world. Eko closes on the line "beings do not obstruct each other," and invites listeners to discover how that already holds in sesshin, even when another person seems to be in the way.

It's nice to see you all and be here with you today.
I had the privilege and honor yesterday to talk to a number of you individually in the Dokusan room.
It's a wonderful practice.
I'm always thinking of good advice that I should follow: "Oh yeah, I should do that.
It would be good, yeah."
But one question that keeps coming up, and that I bring up frequently of late, is the simple question of, in this situation, what really will help?
Will help all beings.
Will help everyone in this situation.

Seeing as carefully as I can all the conditioning, mine and others, and knowing how consequences flow from action, seeing the human being suffering, knowing how my own ego gets in the way of things, seeing all that as clearly as I can, then asking the question, what will help here?
Seeing that I'm allowed myself to guide me, and I think it's useful.
What helps?
What would actually help?
Not my standard idea of what helps and not what a helpful person is supposed to do, but what would actually help?
What can people hear?
How can we connect?
So, that simple question.
And the answer, of course, is not that important.
It's just bringing about the mind that asks that question, that wants to know and then wants to engage in that way.
For me, that's a touchstone these days.
So when I get up here to talk, and when Tim and I decide what we're going to talk about, we have to come back to that question: what's actually helpful?
What's actually useful?
Is this old guy, old Chinese guy Hong Zhe, is it actually helpful to talk about him?
We hope so.
I'm going to make a case for that today.
But I think what's most important in all of this, and this is a line from Hong Zhe, is "let go of adornments and become genuine."
So if I can sit in the seat and together we can let go of adornments and become genuine, then I think that's helpful.
Nothing more is needed than that.
And this Hong Zhe character is, I mean, he's not even the main old guy, right?
He's a secondary old guy.
Why is it that we take him up?
I think we do it simply because for me he's inspiring.
When I read these words, something lights up for me, in my mind, in my heart.
And that's enough, right?
Something lights up.
When I read these images, I want to hear these images, absorb them.
So maybe we can appreciate him in that regard.
He also has practical instructions for meditation, and he's directly in the line of the development of our school.
But for me, the reason to really uphold him is these, as Teigen says, the poetic expression of the awakened mind.
So what is this awakened mind?
We talk about it, but discursive words aren't that useful in expressing the awakened mind.
And sometimes these poetic images, I think, are the closest we can come.
Tim talked some about history yesterday and why we might be concerned with it.
And I think, if I remember correctly, Tim, you had three kinds of truth: historical, devotional, and practical.
I thought that was a nice way to do it.
So there are these stories of history that we have, but that's only one part of the truth.
So what is true there that's apart from this story of a historical development?
I find myself to be ahistorical, I'm deciding, in that it doesn't matter when it was or who said it.
If it's alive, if it lights up something in me, then I'm ready to work with it, ready to hold it up.
As Hungier says, *one beam of light's gleam permeates the vastness.* One beam permeating the vastness.

I have to confess that this chant that we're doing at noon, Guide Posts for the Hall of Pure Bliss, is something that back in Minnesota, where I grew up in Zen, we chanted often at the noonday service.
Also, a similar poem, Guide Posts for the Hall of Silent Illumination.
Just for your information, the House of Silent Illumination is also the Hall of Pure Bliss.
You can rest easy on that.
But I bring it up because these phrases have stuck with me.
This one gleam of, one beam of light's gleam permeating the vastness.
And the flowers of our gazing and listening dropping away.
These images have just penetrated my practice being.
So when Tim brought up the possibility of Hungier, I said, "Oh yeah, that would be good, I like that."
Another way I'm thinking about this expression of the awakened mind is the undivided mind.
What is the activity of the undivided mind?
I'm going to talk about that some more.
The image that Taigen emphasizes in his book related to Hungier is cultivating the empty field.
This empty field is a tantalizing image.
And I think it's an empty field, but it's also the field of boundless emptiness, which, as we know, is not absence of everything, but it's non-separation and interconnection and potentiality.
So this empty field is a very rich field.
There's a suburb of Minneapolis called Richfield, and my teacher used to always go, "About the rich field, you know."
It's not a very interesting suburb, but I think the Mall of America might, no, that's Bloomington, but it's right next door to Richfield.
But this empty field is a very rich field.
It is the house of silent illumination.
We talk about extending this field image.
We sometimes speak of a Buddha field, the Buddha field, a Buddha field.
One definition of that is the field in which a Buddha manifests.
And that's a pretty big field, right?
There are some Mahayana sutras that talk about multiple Buddhas and multiple Buddha fields, but I think that's behind us for the moment.
But this field, this is the Buddha field, the field of boundless awareness.
So it is what we inhabit.
It's that rich field of possibility and non-separation.
I often, in Dokusan, find myself going like this, this big field, you know.
It holds everything.
I think that's one reason I like this image of the field: it holds everything.
There's no choosing required.
No picking and selecting and discriminating.
Everything is held.
Everything is worthy of our kind and careful attention.
You just dip into Taigen a little bit here about the field, or dip into Hong-Ju, I should say.
Hong-Ju says,
*When the stains from old habits are exhausted, the original light appears, blazing through your skull, not admitting any other matters.

Vast and spacious, like sky and water merging during autumn, like snow and moon having the same color, this field is without boundary, beyond direction, magnificently one entity without edge or seam.*
So as you encounter Hong-Ju's poems, there's a little clue here about some of that imagery.
Vast and spacious, like sky and water merging during autumn.
That comes up several places, like snow and moon having the same color.
These things are the same color, merging but distinct.
This field is without boundary, beyond direction, magnificently one entity without edge or seam.
I think this field is what we honor, commemorate, when we set up this practice field of our sesshin.
It's what we actualize.
We bring to life the vast Buddha field by setting up this field of practice.
And isn't this field just feeling very supportive these days, right?
Our meal service is fluid now and elegant, and people have their duties pretty much in hand.

Together we are creating this rich field of practice that holds everything, that is always there, but that we actualize, bring to life, bring into visible awareness when we come together and practice.
Now Hongzhi is also a meditation master, if you will, and one of the precursors of Dogen, as Tim was saying yesterday, particularly in regard to Dogen's teaching of Shikantaza.

Hongzhi's similar teaching is that of silent illumination, and he's really talking about a mode beyond meditation, but it's what we do when we do Zazen, as we practice silent illumination according to Hongzhi's language.
In prosaic terms, that is simply the objectless, themeless, non-dual meditation.
But that is pretty prosaic and dry and abstract.
So today I'm using the activity of the undivided mind.
Maybe that's vivid, the activity of the undivided.
But if you're into that kind of thing, you can be more specific about it.
This is Taigen now talking about Hongzhi's silent illumination.
*Silent illumination involves withdrawal from exclusive focus on a particular sensory or mental object, to allow intent apprehension of all phenomena as a unified totality.*

This comes up in each of our meditation and in discussion with students about meditation: how to concentrate the mind, how to experience some silence and yet open to this vast field, open to this apprehension of all phenomena as a unified totality.

*This objectless meditation aims at a radical, refined non-dualism that does not grasp at any of the highly subtle distinctions to which our familiar mental workings are prone and which estranges us from our experience.*
So this mind is not grasping all of these conceptual frameworks which we are prone to using and which estranges us from our direct, immediate, genuine experience.
So that's Dogen echoes that, or Hongzhi is echoing Dogen.
If we can reverse the time frame.
This is the heart of our practice, another expression of it.
Silence and illumination coming together, it's not unlike the teaching of calm and insight working together, right?
Samatha and Vipassana working together.
Their relationship is subtle between the two, I believe, and something for endless exploration.

It's as if we cultivate silence, or we cultivate a calm, a settledness, and then we allow this insight to occur, we allow the light to emerge, we allow illumination to appear, and one supports the other.
They're really not separate, but our mind separates things.
It's helpful to say, well, yes, there is this silence that we settle into using our breath, using our body, allowing things to be as they are.
And then something is illuminated that we don't have to worry about.
Something is illuminated that shifts the way we meet our life.
Let me read a little bit from the guideposts for silent illumination.
Again, this is a poetic presentation of this central practice of Soto Zen.
He's using the two terms, silence and illumination, as complementary and working together to awaken us.
*Only silence is the supreme speech, only illumination the universal response, responding without falling into achievement, speaking without involving listeners, playing back and forth.
The 10,000 forms majestically glisten and expound the Dharma.
All objects certify it, everyone in dialogue.
Dialoguing and certifying, they respond appropriately to each other.*
It's easy to get lost in all these words.
But this line: the 10,000 forms majestically glisten and expound the Dharma.
That's another central teaching of Dogen, right, that everything, inanimate objects, expound the Dharma.
It's a teaching of [unclear: "Brumsan"] too, but it's central to Soto Zen.
So everything is glistening and expounding the Dharma, if we open our minds to see and hear it.
*But if illumination neglects serenity, then aggressiveness appears.
And if serenity neglects illumination, murkiness leads to wasted Dharma.*
So one without the other is not skillful, and tips us over to one extreme or the other.
But this term that Hongzhi uses, silence, needs a little bit of support, I think, because it sounds like we're just all becoming quiet and empty and still and nothing else.
We need to be careful, and I think we are attuned to that these days in our practice.
So let me read something more here.
Again, just let this flow.
Silence and illumination, in this case he's using slightly different words, stillness and wisdom.
*So it is said that our delusional, normal thinking stops, and stillness or concentration arises necessarily.*
For a little while, for a moment, for a longer period.
*Stillness arises and wisdom appears.*
Some new way, some shift in how we meet our lives.
*Wisdom arises and stillness necessarily disappears in active functioning.*
So we don't need to cling to stillness, right?
We can immerse ourselves in the functioning of our lives and not just cling to this blissful stillness that we might or might not discover from time to time.
This silence, and Hongzhi refers to it at the end of that guidepost for the Hall of Pure Bliss, he refers to it explicitly as Vimalakirti silence.
If you know the Vimalakirti Sutra, you know that it ends something with Manjusri posing some question, and Vimalakirti's response is this mythical thunderous silence, right?
Thunderous silence.
And Vimalakirti, you may know, was anything but removed.
He was completely engaged in the world.
He was a lay person.
He was always showing up where he wasn't expected, certainly.
He's showing up with the disciples and the bodhisattvas and pestering them about what they're doing.
That's not really the true Dharma, is it?
They get all flustered, and he expounds what they should be doing, how they should be praying.
So the bodhisattvas and the disciples are kind of annoyed by him, and they avoid him.
But normal beings, he's always in their midst and helping.
So Vimalakirti's thunderous silence is completely engaged in the world.
Again, these images of the undivided mind: just allow them to light up your mind, or not.
And as they come and go, appreciate whatever light they bring.
The guidepost for the Hall of Pure Bliss starts out like this.
*By seeking appearances and sounds, one cannot truly find the way.*
So that's pretty straightforward.
If we're chasing after the normal things we chase after, we cannot truly find the way.
*The deep source of realization comes with constancy, bliss, self, and purity.*
What the heck does that mean, really?
These are kind of abstract terms, and clearly someone has a definition of them somewhere, and someone has concocted a way in which their defined terms interrelate.
We could spend time on that, but I don't think we need to.
One of the things I find myself advocating recently is: don't find something in the teachings with which to argue and thereby dismiss all the other truth that might be there.
It's like, oh, we hear this thing, and oh, but this thing about bliss and self, what the heck is that?
I don't get that.
And we possibly focus on this thing that we want to argue with and close up to the rest of it.
So I find myself encouraging students: don't argue with the teaching.
Find out what's true.
Discover what is true there.
I think it's a slightly different attitude.
So I offer that to us as we read these sometimes strange-sounding teaching poems.
Don't try to find things to argue with.
Be illuminated by what you discover to be true in these teachings.
One thing Hongzhi is doing is trying to capture how it all fits together somehow.

We use these terms like, well, okay, everything is interconnected and all one, yes, and then we have the myriad dharmas and the ten thousand things that are multiple, yes, and somehow the two are not two and not one, right?
This is important, but it's difficult.
And Hongzhi has some, I think, felicitous, if you will, expressions of this, that when I hear them, I can't explain it, but yes, that holds it and honors it as together.
So I think there are some of those in this poem, Guideposts for the Hall of Pure Bliss, to let me indulge a little bit and continue with that.
*Catching the opportunity to emerge amid transformations, it flourishes.*
Now, this is kind of complicated language in a way, but if we open to it, this "it" that is timeless and unified flourishes amid transformations.
So the one flourishing amidst transformations.
I can see that.
I can work with that, right?
*All dharmas transcend their limits.
All gates are wide open.
Through the open gates are the byways of playful wandering.*
Another phrase that has always stuck with me.
Let me skip ahead to what I want to end with today.
That is a particular praise of Hongzhi's, a particular teaching from these [unclear: "practice of instructions"].
I'll just read the first part of it.
*Separate yourself from disturbance and face whatever appears before you.
Not one iota seeps through from outside.
The two forms, yin and yang, have the same root, and the 10,000 images have one substance.
Following change and going along with transformation, the whole is not clouded over by previous conditions.
Then you reach the foundation of the great freedom.
Wind blows and moon shines, and beings do not obstruct each other.*
So we could spend a long time on just those phrases, but the one I want to highlight is, beings do not obstruct each other.
This is one that we would tend to argue with, right?
I mean, what are you talking about?
Look at fighting and war and selfishness, and there's obstruction all over the place.
But okay, this is an expression of the undivided mind, perhaps.
Beings do not obstruct each other.
So rather than argue with that, how can we discover the truth of that?

How is it that beings, and again this is an expression of the whole thing, it's not that there are no beings, there are beings, and they're all over the place, and they're interacting, and yet they do not obstruct each other?
How could that be when it seems so obvious that it is otherwise?
So here's a good place to practice that.
Don't argue with the teaching.
Discover the truth.
That means: do not obstruct each other.
How could that be even?
They interact, and they respond to each other, right?
We could say that.
And they are in this vast and subtle interplay that is in one sense undivided, in another sense active and functioning, Dogen's teaching of Zenki, or total dynamic functioning.
So it's another expression of that.
So there are beings that are interacting and responding, but perhaps they're not obstructing each other.
Perhaps this is the workings of the one inexpressible.
How can we return to this sesshin and inhabit this Buddha field and do this practice where beings don't obstruct each other?
In sesshin it's a little easier to see, right?
Not that it's that obvious, because you might find yourself obstructed by another being during sesshin.
Then you might decide, well, this person isn't doing what they're supposed to be doing, and therefore they're obstructing me, and then I can't do what I'm supposed to do.
And there's obstructions all over the place, even in this lovely thing that we do.
So here's a chance to practice.
Beings do not obstruct each other.
And it's a little easier to see because we can let go.
Here we're cultivating that silence and that illumination.
We can let go and inhabit this field of non-obstruction, of beings not obstructing each other.
And then by extension, our whole world: can it be true?
Yes, there's something there.
Beings do not obstruct each other.
How is that true?
It doesn't mean that it doesn't matter, that suffering doesn't matter.
Of course it matters, but on some level beings do not obstruct each other.

And when we live from that point of view, our response in that interplay can be a little more elegant and gracious and kind, because we are not so concerned about apparent obstructions, but we're concerned about kindness and clarity and helping all beings.
So I started out with: what is it that really helps?
And then ending with this challenging teaching of beings do not obstruct each other.
We don't need to figure it out.
We just need to discover how it already is true in this sesshin and in this big wide Buddha field that has no edge, no boundary.
